description: A website for discovering existing origami patterns and tutorials, then helping users turn a requested object or uploaded reference photo into an origami crease pattern or step-by-step instructions.

questions.question: Which language should the Next.js website use?

options.label: TypeScript
options.description: Recommended for a typed Next.js application.

questions.rationale: Next.js is explicitly requested; TypeScript is a practical default for a multi-step interactive interface.

questions.question: Which frontend framework should the website use?

options.label: Next.js
options.description: The requested React framework for the website.

questions.question: What should the first version's website experience include (for example: text prompt, photo upload, generated crease diagram, step-by-step instructions, source attribution, saved projects)?
questions.recommendedChoice: Text prompt and photo upload; show generated crease pattern or instructions with source attribution; allow download, with saved projects optional.
questions.rationale: These capabilities follow the request; prioritize the MVP and indicate whether accounts/saved projects are needed.

questions.question: Which language should power the origami and ingestion API?

options.label: Python
options.description: The requested language, well suited to image processing and computational geometry.

questions.question: Which framework should expose the Python API?

options.label: Azure Functions
options.description: Azure's serverless API option; an explicitly chosen custom framework can be entered instead.

questions.rationale: FastAPI is a suitable Python API default for image uploads and long-running generation jobs; confirm or choose another framework.

questions.question: Which generation capabilities should the first version provide, and should it produce validated crease patterns, folding instructions, or both? Please note any expected limits for uploaded photos or generation time.
questions.recommendedChoice: Support text prompts and photo uploads; return either an available, rights-cleared pattern/tutorial match or an explicitly labeled generated result; provide beginner-friendly steps and a downloadable crease diagram, with limitations clearly shown.
questions.rationale: Text-to-object and photo-to-origami may require different algorithms and validation; scope the first release realistically.

questions.question: Which language should the source-ingestion worker use?

options.label: Python
options.description: Shares libraries and models with the Python API.

questions.rationale: The requested Python stack and shared origami processing libraries make Python the natural worker language.

questions.question: How should the ingestion worker be implemented?

options.label: Python background worker
options.description: A queued worker that fetches permitted sources, extracts metadata, and records attribution.

questions.rationale: Periodic crawling and parsing should run out of the web request path; confirm the desired worker approach.

questions.question: What acquisition rules should ingestion follow? Please specify whether to use only publisher APIs/feeds or explicitly licensed sources, whether arbitrary-site scraping is allowed, and how to handle robots.txt, terms of service, rate limits, attribution, takedown requests, and copyrighted images/instructions.
questions.recommendedChoice: Use an allowlist of sources with APIs/feeds or explicit permission/licenses; honor robots.txt, terms, and rate limits; store source URLs and license/attribution metadata; do not republish copyrighted diagrams or tutorial text without permission; provide a takedown process.
questions.rationale: The ingestion scope must respect source rights and site policies; confirm the allowed acquisition and storage policy.

questions.question: Which storage does the application need?

options.label: PostgreSQL
options.description: Store source catalog metadata, jobs, and (if needed) users and saved projects.

options.label: Blob Storage
options.description: Store user-uploaded reference photos and generated crease-pattern files.

options.label: No datastore required
options.description: Choose only if the application will not persist uploaded files, patterns, sources, jobs, or user data.

questions.rationale: Photo uploads and generated files require object storage; a source catalog and asynchronous job records generally require a relational database.

questions.question: Should users sign in to use application API features?

options.label: Yes
options.description: Users authenticate to access account-specific API features such as saved projects.

options.label: No
options.description: Core generation and browsing features are available without signing in.

questions.rationale: Sign-in is not specified; an anonymous MVP reduces friction, with accounts possible if saved projects are required.
